newsitem.title: GERMANY: Growth potential seen in Asian coffee demand.
newsitem.headline: Growth potential seen in Asian coffee demand.

text.p: Coffee demand in Asia was set to rise over the next few years and beyond, reflecting a higher acceptance of westernised life styles, independent coffee consultant Mick Wheeler said on Tuesday.

Wheeler, who was addressing the F.O. Licht world coffee conference, said his analysis of 20 countries in the region showed total consumption could rise to 14.9 million bags in the year 2000 compared with 13 million bags now.
"The outlook for the region is fairly bright...I see the region's share of world consumption growing from presently 14.8 percent to 15.5 percent in the year 2000," he said.
Wheeler said he was optimistic for Chinese demand growth, but it would not develop at a very rapid pace.

"By 2000, the Chinese could be consuming 350,000-400,000 bags compared with an estimated 210,000 bags at the moment, but I disagree with forecasts going into millions of bags just on the strength of population numbers," he said.
China is a tea culture and coffee would take some time to be established, he believed.
The coffee industry should stress the convenience aspect of instant coffee, which already accounted for 70-75 percent of Chinese consumption, as preparation was similar to that of tea.
"Chinese consumers are also looking for all-in-one convenience products with milk and sugar already added as this offers them consistency of preparation," Wheeler said.
Japan's consumption in 2000 might rise to 6.8 million bags in 2000 from 6.1 million bags in 1995 as the market was coming closer to saturation.
But it was a success story in which a premium product with high prices had captured the imagination of consumers, who responded to U.S. style products and marketing.
Unlike Europe, where younger consumers were moving away from coffee, U.S. style gourmet coffees were becoming especially popular with 25-39 year old Japanese men.
Japan is often seen as the trendsetter for future Asian consumption patterns.
Wheeler said Austrialia's coffee consumption may rise to 880,000 bags in 2000 from 775,000 presently and New Zealands's might advance to 155,000 bags from 140,000 in the same period.
South Korean use might grow to 1.3 million bags from 1.1 million now, while Hong Kong, Pakistan, Taiwan and North Korea should remain fairly static.
